prompt: In the `PropDrilling` demo, which component declares `unit` as a prop and never uses it?
hint: Its own comment says so.

choices.text: `DrillLeaf`
choices.why: It uses `unit` twice: to decide whether to divide by 60, and to print the word.

choices.text: `PropDrilling`, which only writes `unit="hours"`
choices.why: `PropDrilling` sets the value; it passes `unit` as an attribute on `DrillMiddle` and declares no props at all.

choices.text: `DrillMiddle`, the component drawing the list
choices.why: Right. It names `unit` in its props and passes it on in its template, and does nothing else with it.

choices.text: Both `DrillMiddle` and `DrillLeaf`
choices.why: The leaf is the one component that reads `unit`, which is why the value had to reach it.

prompt: Which of these are ambient values in the lesson's sense, the kind drilling makes a problem of? Choose all that apply.
hint: Needed at many depths, set in one place for all of them.

choices.text: The minutes of one session, passed to the row that draws it
choices.why: That value belongs to one row and is its reason to exist; a prop is the right way to send it.

choices.text: A theme for a whole part of the tree
choices.why: Right. A setting that applies to a subtree, set once for every component in it.

choices.text: The current user, which every component of a feature reads
choices.why: Right. A service a whole feature uses is the second kind the lesson lists.

choices.text: The active tab of a tab group, shared with its tabs
choices.why: Right. Components of one library sharing state among themselves is the third kind.

prompt: In the `PropDrilling` transcript, what number does the leaf for the 45-minute session show?
hint: It divides by 60 when the unit is hours.

prompt: In the `ProvideInject` demo, what does `InjectMiddle` declare as props?
hint: Compare it with `DrillMiddle`.

choices.text: `sessions` and `unit`, as `DrillMiddle` did
choices.why: That was the drilled version. The point of the provided one is that the middle stops naming the unit.

choices.text: No props: the sessions are injected too
choices.why: Only the unit is provided. The sessions are still a prop, from the parent that owns them.

choices.text: `unitKey`, so the leaves can find the value
choices.why: The key is imported from `keys.js` by whoever provides or injects; the middle does neither.

choices.text: `sessions`, the list it draws, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. It draws the list and never mentions a unit at all.

prompt: The whole planner provides `'minutes'` under `unitKey`, and one panel inside it provides `'hours'` under the same key. What does a leaf inside that panel inject?
hint: An inject looks at the nearest ancestor that provided the key.

choices.text: `'hours'`
choices.why: Right. The panel's value sits on top of the planner's and hides it, for the panel's subtree only.

choices.text: `'minutes'`, because the first provider wins
choices.why: Nearer wins, not earlier. That is what makes provide a way to override for a subtree.

choices.text: Nothing, and Vue warns that the key was provided twice
choices.why: Providing the same key at two depths is allowed and is the point of the override; there is no such warning.

choices.text: Whichever of the two changed most recently
choices.why: Neither value changes here. Which provider answers is decided by the tree, not by time.

prompt: A leaf calls `inject(unitKey)` inside a click handler rather than at the top level of its `<script setup>`. It is below the provider. What happens when the button is clicked?
hint: The two rules in this section are about timing.

choices.text: It gets `'hours'`, since the leaf is below the provider
choices.why: Being below the provider is one of the two rules, and only one. The call has to happen during setup as well.

choices.text: Vue warns that inject only works in setup, and nothing comes back
choices.why: Right. During a click there is no component being set up to attach the call to, so Vue warns and the inject returns nothing.

choices.text: It gets the value the provider held when the leaf was first set up
choices.why: That is what an inject during setup gives. Later, there is nothing to look the key up from.

choices.text: The click handler throws, and the page stops responding
choices.why: Vue does not throw here; it warns in the console, and the handler carries on with nothing.

prompt: A component `Panel` calls `provide(unitKey, 'hours')`. Which of these can inject it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Below, at any depth. Nowhere else.

choices.text: The component that renders `Panel`
choices.why: That is the provider's parent, which is above it. A value is found only below the provider.

choices.text: A component four levels inside `Panel`
choices.why: Right. Depth does not matter, and the components in between need not know.

choices.text: A sibling of `Panel`, rendered beside it
choices.why: A sibling is not below `Panel`, so it sees whatever its own ancestors provide.

choices.text: A direct child of `Panel`
choices.why: Right. A child is the nearest place below the provider.

prompt: In the `ReactiveProvide` transcript, after `Add five` and then the direct write of 999, what total does the provider show?
hint: One of the two clicks was refused.

prompt: A provider holds `const total = ref(75)` and calls `provide(totalKey, total.value)`. Later it adds five to `total`. What does a component that injected `totalKey` show?
hint: `provide` hands over whatever it is given, once.

choices.text: 75, and it stays 75
choices.why: Right. `total.value` was read once, at the call. To follow the changes, provide the ref itself.

choices.text: 80, because provided values are reactive
choices.why: Provide does not make anything reactive. It handed over the number 75, and a number does not follow a ref.

choices.text: Nothing, with a warning that `.value` cannot be provided
choices.why: A plain number is a perfectly good value to provide; Vue accepts it without a word.

choices.text: 75 until the injector re-renders for some other reason, then 80
choices.why: A re-render reads the same injected number again. Nothing ever gave the injector the ref.

prompt: Change the demo so the provider calls `provide(plannerKey, { total, addFive })`, with no `readonly`. What does the badge's `Write to it directly` do now?
hint: Look at the second row of the section's table.

choices.text: It is still refused, since an injected ref is read-only
choices.why: Only `readonly` refuses a write. A ref handed over as it is accepts one from anybody who holds it.

choices.text: The badge and the provider both show 999, through the one ref
choices.why: Right. The badge holds the provider's own ref and writes to it, and the owner is not told who did it.

choices.text: Only the badge shows 999; the provider keeps its own total
choices.why: There is one ref, not a copy per injector, so a write through it is seen everywhere.

choices.text: Vue warns that a child mutated a provided value, and applies it
choices.why: That warning is for props. A provided ref has no rule of its own, which is why the provider adds `readonly`.

prompt: To give injectors a view of a ref that follows every change and accepts none, the provider wraps it: `___(total)`.
hint: The function the demo imports beside `ref` and `provide`.

prompt: Why does the lesson provide under a Symbol rather than a string like `'unit'`?
hint: What does `Symbol('unit') === Symbol('unit')` print?

choices.text: Vue 3.5 refuses a string key
choices.why: A string key still works, and the documentation's shortest examples use one.

choices.text: A Symbol makes the provided value reactive
choices.why: Reactivity comes from what is provided, a ref or a `computed`, never from the key.

choices.text: Two Symbols are never equal, so nobody else's provide answers for it
choices.why: Right. Only code that imports that exact Symbol reaches the value; two equal strings are the same key.

choices.text: A lookup by Symbol is faster than one by string
choices.why: Speed is not the reason the lesson gives, and the difference would not show.

prompt: What does keeping every key in one `keys.js` give, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things, each for somebody reading or changing the code.

choices.text: A place to give each key the type of its value
choices.why: Right. Lesson 16 does it with `InjectionKey`.

choices.text: A check, when the app is built, that every injected key has a provider
choices.why: Nothing checks that. A missing provider shows up at run time, as `undefined` and a warning, or as the default.

choices.text: A list of everything provided, in one file
choices.why: Right. Provide is not visible in the template, so this file is where a reader starts.

choices.text: One name to search for to find every provider and injector
choices.why: Right. A search for `unitKey` finds them all, where `'unit'` would be buried among everything else.

choices.text: Values provided under those keys become read-only
choices.why: Read-only is what `readonly` gives, applied to the value. The file holds keys, not values.

prompt: In `keys.js`, somebody changes `Symbol('unit')` to `Symbol('display unit')` and touches nothing else. What changes when the app runs?
hint: Is the description the key, or a label on it?

choices.text: Every `inject(unitKey)` stops finding the value until it is renamed too
choices.why: The components import `unitKey`, the variable, and it still holds the one Symbol both sides use.

choices.text: The app breaks, since a description may not contain a space
choices.why: A description is any string; it is there for people, in messages and in the console.

choices.text: Components that used the string `'unit'` now find a different value
choices.why: A Symbol never equals a string, whatever its description says, so no string key was ever involved.

choices.text: Only the text of a warning, or a log line, that names the key
choices.why: Right. Provider and injector still share one Symbol; the description is what `injection "Symbol(...)" not found` prints.

prompt: In the `Orphan` demo, with nothing above it, what does `inject(unitKey, 'minutes')` give?
hint: Look at the second line of the page, and at the warnings above it.

choices.text: `undefined`, and a warning
choices.why: That is the first inject, with no second argument. A default changes both halves.

choices.text: `'minutes'`, and no warning
choices.why: Right. A default says that being used without a provider is expected, so Vue has nothing to warn about.

choices.text: `'minutes'`, with a warning that no provider was found
choices.why: There was one warning in the transcript, and it came from the inject without a default.

choices.text: An error, since `unitKey` was never provided anywhere
choices.why: A missing provider is never an error in Vue; it is `undefined` or the default.

prompt: With no provider, what does `inject('settings', () => ({ weekStartsOn: 'Monday' }))` return? It has no third argument.
hint: The third argument says the function is a factory rather than the value.

choices.text: The object `{ weekStartsOn: 'Monday' }`
choices.why: That is what the demo got, and it passed `true` as well. Without it, Vue does not call the function.

choices.text: `undefined`, and a warning naming `settings`
choices.why: A second argument is present, so this is a default and no warning is given; it is just the wrong default.

choices.text: The arrow function itself
choices.why: Right. Without `true`, the second argument is the value, and here the value is a function. `made.weekStartsOn` would then be `undefined`.

choices.text: An error, because a default must not be a function
choices.why: A function is an acceptable default value; that is exactly why the third argument is needed to say which is meant.

prompt: A `FormField` injects the form it belongs to, and cannot work without it. Which answer for a missing provider does the lesson's table give?
hint: A field outside a form is a bug.

choices.text: An empty form object, so the field still draws
choices.why: That hides the bug: the field looks fine and submits to nothing. It is the silent failure the lesson warns about.

choices.text: A default that degrades visibly, like the course's id
choices.why: That is for a nice-to-have, such as the titles. A field without its form is not degraded, it is broken.

choices.text: The usual value, as with a unit
choices.why: A form has no usual value to fall back on; every field belongs to a particular one.

choices.text: No default, and a clear error
choices.why: Right. Something the component cannot work without is better found at once.

prompt: Why does `SessionRow` write `titles?.value[session.course]` in its script, with `.value`?
hint: The template and the script treat a ref differently.

choices.text: An injected ref is unwrapped in the template only, never in the script
choices.why: Right. `titles` is the `computed` that `App` provided, and in the script it is read through `.value`.

choices.text: `inject` returns a copy, and `.value` reaches the original
choices.why: Inject returns the very `computed` that was provided; there is no copy to get past.

choices.text: `.value` makes the row follow the titles when they arrive
choices.why: The row follows the titles because a `computed` is reactive; `.value` is only how the script reads it.

choices.text: Without a provider, `.value` is what holds the default
choices.why: Without a provider `titles` is `null`, which is why the `?.` is there, and the row falls back to the id.

prompt: According to the section's table, how should a value shared by the whole application and changed from many places be passed?
hint: The last row of the table.

choices.text: Provided by `App`, since `App` is above everything
choices.why: It would reach everywhere, and nothing would say who changed it. That is where most "I need provide" ends up being wrong.

choices.text: As props, since drilling is honest
choices.why: Drilling is honest for two or three levels, not for a value the whole application changes.

choices.text: In a store, where one module owns the state and names every change
choices.why: Right. One module owns the state, every change is a named action, and the browser's Vue tools show each one.

choices.text: With `app.provide` in `main.js`
choices.why: That makes a value available everywhere, as a library does, but gives none of the rules a store adds.

prompt: What does a component give up when it injects a value instead of receiving it as a prop? Choose all that apply.
hint: Visibility, portability, easy testing.

choices.text: Its tag no longer shows everything it needs
choices.why: Right. `<SessionRow :session="s" />` looks complete and also needs the titles.

choices.text: An injected ref no longer updates the component
choices.why: An injected ref is followed exactly like one received as a prop; the planner's rows follow the titles when they arrive.

choices.text: Moved outside the provider's subtree, it quietly gets the default
choices.why: Right. The move compiles and runs, which is why the choice of default matters.

choices.text: A test has to provide the value as well
choices.why: Right. Lesson 21 does it with `global.provide`.

hint: The provide and the inject happen during setup; the courses arrive later.
items: Each `SessionRow` calls `inject(titlesKey, null)` in its setup

hint: Down one level, down many, from anywhere, or a name nobody else can use.

pairs.left: the session a row exists to draw
a unit set once for every component in a panel

right_distractors: a string key with a prefix

prompt: `TotalBadge` runs `const { total, addFive } = inject(plannerKey)`. Somebody moves it into the page header, outside the component that provides `plannerKey`. What happens when the page loads?
hint: Work out what `inject` returns there, then what destructuring does with it.

choices.text: It shows `Total:  minutes`, with the number left blank
choices.why: That would need `inject` to return an object with empty fields. It returns `undefined`, which has no fields at all.

choices.text: It still works, since every provided value reaches the whole page
choices.why: Only components below the provider can find it; the header is not below it.

choices.text: It gets a fresh total of 75 of its own
choices.why: Inject never creates the provider's state. Without a provider and without a default there is nothing to get.

choices.text: Vue warns the injection was not found, then destructuring `undefined` throws
choices.why: Right. No default means `undefined` and a warning, and taking `total` out of `undefined` is a TypeError. A default here would have been a choice about what the badge does alone.
